data.title: FanDuel starts off the NFL season with its best Sunday ever
data.description:
FanDuel (FLUT) highlighted that it recorded its biggest NFL regular-season Sunday ever by actives and kicked off the season with a new high for the sportsbook. "Football season is one of the biggest moments on the sports calendar, and this record reflects the incredible energy fans brought to opening weekend," noted the company in a LinkedIn Post.

The strong showing by FanDuel (FLUT) comes in the face of intense competition from prediction market operators Kalshi (KALSHI) and Polymarket (POLYMARKET) for sports betting customers with their contract-based form of wagering on the NFL. The promotional environment with DraftKings (DKNG), BetMGM (MGM) (GMVHF), Fanatics (FANA), Bet365, and Caesars Sportsbook (CZR) has also picked up.

FanDuel Sportsbook is currently live for online wagering in 24 U.S. states plus Washington, D.C., with Arkansas and Missouri the only new markets since the 2025 NFL football season.

Shares of Flutter Entertainment plc. (FLUT) are down more than 50% on a year-to-date basis.

data.title: A history of good and bad tech predictions
data.description:
Technology has a habit of humbling even the smartest people. Some predictions have proved astonishingly accurate, while others have gone spectacularly wrong, a history that Deutsche Bank Research says is worth remembering as the world tries to predict what AI will become.

Bob Metcalfe, co-inventor of Ethernet and founder of 3Com, knows the feeling. In 1995, he predicted that the internet would go “spectacularly supernova” and collapse in 1996. When that failed to happen, he took a copy of his prediction, put it through a blender, and drank it at a conference in 1997.

There have also been some remarkably good calls.

In 1926, scientist Nikola Tesla predicted that wireless technology would allow people to communicate instantly regardless of distance, using instruments simple enough to fit into a vest pocket. Deutsche Bank said Tesla was right, although he was less precise about how or when it would happen.

Ray Kurzweil made another striking prediction in 1999, saying computers would have human-level intelligence by 2029. Deutsche Bank noted that many, though not all, of his predictions have worked out and said his long-standing forecast for artificial general intelligence by the end of this decade is remarkably close to today's “San Francisco Consensus.”

Tech Predictions Over the Century

Year & Speaker Tech Prediction Verdict & Actual Outcome
1926 – N. Tesla Vest-pocket wireless communication GOOD: Accurately described smartphones
1934 – A. Einstein Nuclear energy impossible BAD: Sustained reactor built by 1942
1995 – B. Metcalfe Internet collapse in 1996 BAD: Forced to literally "eat his words"
1999 – R. Kurzweil Human-level AI by 2029 GOOD: On track with current AI forecasts
2007 – S. Ballmer iPhone market failure BAD: Over 3 billion devices sold
2016 – G. Hinton AI replaces radiologists BAD: Radiologist workforce grew 10%

Then there are the misses.

Albert Einstein said in 1934 that there was no indication nuclear energy would ever be obtainable. By 1942, scientists at the University of Chicago had created the first sustained nuclear chain reaction, a precursor to the nuclear reactor.

In 2005, YouTube co-founder Steve Chen said there were not many videos he wanted to watch. A year later, Google (GOOG) (GOOGL) bought YouTube for $1.65B, and the unit later generated more than $11B in advertising revenue in a single quarter, according to Deutsche Bank.

Microsoft (MSFT) CEO Steve Ballmer was similarly dismissive of Apple's (AAPL) iPhone in 2007, saying it had no chance of gaining significant market share. More than 3B iPhones have since been sold, Deutsche Bank said.

AI has already produced its own examples. In 2016, Geoffrey Hinton predicted that deep learning would outperform radiologists within five to 10 years and suggested people should stop training them. Instead, the number of radiologists increased about 10% over the following decade, partly because of AI's limitations and partly because of rising healthcare demand.

Hinton later walked back his comments, with humans and AI increasingly working together.

OpenAI (OPENAI) CEO Sam Altman also revised his 2025 prediction that AI could perform 30%-40% of economic tasks in the not-too-distant future. In May, he said his team had been roughly right about the technology but “pretty wrong” about its economic and social implications.

data.title: The easy money in AI may be over as spending surges beyond revenue
data.description:
The easy money may be gone when it comes to investing in artificial intelligence as the massive capital spending needed to build out AI infrastructure increasingly outpaces revenue growth, according to Joe Albano of Tech Cache.

Albano said he has been closely watching capital expenditures from major technology companies and AI players, including Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft, OpenAI and Anthropic, with spending growth substantially exceeding revenue growth.

The growing gap between investment and revenue is putting pressure on companies’ balance sheets, with cash and free cash flow being depleted and some businesses moving into negative free cash flow.

Albano noted that AI compute requires dramatically more investment than traditional data centers, while companies including Google and Meta have increasingly turned to debt financing and others have raised equity to fund the buildout.

At the same time, the financing environment is becoming more challenging as the AI infrastructure chain expands beyond the largest technology companies toward AI and frontier-model labs with unproven business models and little or no free cash flow.

Albano questioned how long investors will continue funding the enormous upfront costs of AI infrastructure without clearer evidence that these investments are translating into sustainable real-world returns.

Albano said the current AI investment cycle could therefore reach a critical point over the next year. While he acknowledged that the upfront spending required to develop AI is understandable, he argued that investors will eventually need to see “proof of life” from the massive capital being deployed.

Rising costs for components such as DRAM and NAND are also creating additional margin pressure, making the economics of the AI buildout increasingly important to watch.

The shift means investors may need to be more selective rather than simply buying into the broader AI theme.

As the market moves beyond the initial phase of enthusiasm and easy gains, Albano's view is that the sustainability of AI spending, access to financing and the ability of companies to eventually generate cash from their investments will become increasingly important factors for investors.

data.title: TORM prices $290M secondary share offering
data.description:
• TORM (TRMD) said on Tuesday that OCM Njord Holdings priced a secondary offering of 9M Class A shares at $32.25/share for gross proceeds of about $290.3M.
  • OCM Njord Holdings is indirectly owned by funds managed by Oaktree Capital Management and affiliates.
  • The underwriter has a 30-day option to purchase up to 1.35M additional shares from the selling shareholder, which currently owns about 20% of TORM’s Class A shares. 
  • The transaction is expected to close on Sept. 16.
  • J.P. Morgan Securities LLC is acting as the sole underwriter for the offering.

data.title: NIQ expands GeoPurchase offering to five European markets
data.description:
• NIQ (NIQ)  launched Digital Purchase GeoAudiences across France, Germany, Italy, Spain and the U.K.
  • The offering extends NIQ’s GeoPurchase capabilities into digital-first categories, including travel, automotive, technology, telecommunications, and financial services.
  • the new offering combines NIQ’s digital commerce data with geographic insights to help advertisers identify areas with stronger digital shopping activity and use those signals to guide media planning and spending.
  • NIQ operates in more than 90 countries, covering about 82% of the global population and more than $7.4T in consumer spending.

data.title: Amazon sets dates for its Prime Big Deal Days shopping event
data.description:
Amazon (AMZN) plans to hold its 2026 Prime Big Deal Days sale on October 6–7, beginning at 12:01 a.m. Pacific time. The 48-hour event is limited to Prime members and will feature “millions” of discounts across electronics, home goods, fashion, beauty, toys, groceries, and Amazon devices. The Seattle-based e-commerce giant noted well over one million items will be at their lowest price of the year to date.

As part of the Prime Big Deal Days sales event, Amazon (AMZN) will fire off discounts of 45% or more on selected Sony (SONY), Tarte, and Adidas (ADDYY) products, as well as up to 45% off fall apparel and shoes and up to 35% off bedding, blankets, and holiday décor. Some Halloween costumes and accessories will be listed starting at $5. 

Amazon (AMZN) is also using the event to promote its broader membership ecosystem. Pre-event offers include Prime Card rewards; discounts tied to American Express and Mercury points; a $20 Grubhub promotion; reduced-price digital subscriptions; and a $1,500 Amazon gift card for qualifying new-vehicle purchases or leases through Amazon Autos. 

Amazon (AMZN) has run the same basic fall, Prime-member-only sales event every year since 2022 under different names. 

Shares of Amazon (AMZN) trickled 0.4% lower in premarket action on Tuesday after slipping 1.3% on Monday.

data.title: Strawberry Fields REIT buys hospital campus in Missouri
data.description:
• Strawberry Fields REIT (STRW) has bought a hospital campus in Marshall, Missouri.
  • The campus comprises a 60-bed hospital, 99-bed skilled nursing facility and medical office building. It was added to an existing master lease with an affiliate of American Medical Administrators; formally known as Reliant Care Group.
  • Following the acquisition, the company owns and leases 21 healthcare facilities in Missouri.
  • Moishe Gubin, the company's chairman & CEO, noted: “I am pleased to announce that we closed this deal and continue growing in Missouri. As I mentioned in our earnings call last month, acquisition activity began slowly this year. With this transaction completed and several additional transactions under consideration, we hope to finish the year on a strong note."

data.title: BOXABL names Larry King as CFO and Heather Clayton as CAO
data.description:
• BOXABL (BXBL) said on Tuesday it appointed Larry King as CFO and Heather Clayton as Chief Accounting Officer.
  • King brings more than 35 years of finance, accounting, and operations experience, including SEC reporting, M&A, and operational turnarounds.
  • He previously served as CFO of Chukchansi Gold Resort & Casino and Riviera Holdings.
  • Clayton brings nearly 10 years of finance and accounting experience, including senior roles as CFO of ASTOUND Group and the Vegas Golden Knights.
  • Share +1.02%
